Sultan Haidar Ali Datasheet as part of RadioLink for Team 105

Submission: 10, 26, 2026

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This datasheet documents the hub subsystem of RadioLink, Team 105's embedded project.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text: RadioLink is a hub-and-spoke system, and this board is the hub. It has an on-board OLED for graphics, a debug LED, and three UART ports. Board 1 carries the microphone, board 2 carries the pushbuttons and a temperature sensor, and board 3 carries the speaker. The microphone and button boards send their data to the hub. The hub shows a custom interface on the OLED, which is navigated with board 2's buttons, and it plays the microphone signal through the speaker.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
My work on RadioLink has centered on concept ideation, user-needs benchmarking, and the hub itself. The hub receives the microphone and temperature data, presents it on a custom OLED interface that is navigated with the pushbuttons, and sends the microphone signal to the speaker.

  • Block Diagram
  • Component Selection

  • Schematic
  • Power Budget

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This block diagram is the hub of RadioLink, Team 105's hub-and-spoke design. A PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano sits at the center. The 9 V input is regulated to 5 V by an LM7805CT. An MCP1700-3302E/TO makes 3.3 V from that rail for the EastRising ER-OLED0.96-1.3W. I2C between the microcontroller and the display is level-shifted with 2N7000 MOSFETs. A debug LED is driven from RA2.

Three UART ports connect the hub to the other boards. Each link is 5 V and uses an RX/TX pair:

  • Connector 1: RX on RC3, TX on RC2
  • Connector 2: RX on RF1, TX on RF0
  • Connector 3: RX on RA4, TX on RA3

The microphone board and the button and temperature board send data in. The hub shows that information on the OLED, which is navigated with board 2's buttons, and it sends the microphone signal out to the speaker board.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
The hub PCB is meant to be assembled, soldered, inspected, and repaired by hand. Through-hole packages are preferred wherever they are practical. The OLED module is an intentional exception, because that display assembly is not a discrete through-hole part.

Four parts were selected against that rule: the display module, the 9 V to 5 V regulator, the I2C level-shift MOSFETs, and the 5 V to 3.3 V regulator. SSD1306 is the controller inside the display. It is not the orderable module.

docs.title: OLED Display
docs.text:
Requirements: A readable graphic display for the hub UI, small enough for this board, with an I2C interface the PIC18F57Q43 can drive. Logic supply must work from the 3.3 V rail. The module may be a flex-connected assembly. It does not have to be through-hole.

SSD1306 names the controller IC. The orderable part is the EastRising module that uses that controller.

docs.title: Option 3: ER-OLED0.96-1.3W
docs.text:
• $2.49 each
  • Link to product
  • Series datasheet

This is an EastRising 0.96-inch, 128 x 64, white OLED module with a top-contact FPC. The controller on the module is an SSD1306. The module is not a breakout board.

EastRising lists VDD as 1.65 V to 3.3 V, typical 2.8 V. Logic-high is 0.8 x VDD. With the internal charge pump enabled, VBAT is specified as 3.5 V to 4.2 V. IDD is 180 µA typical and 300 µA maximum. With the charge pump generating VCC, IBAT at 100% of the pixels on is 25.6 mA typical and 32.0 mA maximum (datasheet Note 8: VDD = 2.8 V, generated VCC = 7.25 V). The framebuffer is 128 x 64 bits, which is 1 KB.

Pros Cons SSD1306 controller, with I2C available on this module 0.96-inch screen is small 128 x 64 FPC assembly, not through-hole $2.49, and it was available to order 1 KB framebuffer Logic supply accepts 3.3 V Charge-pump VBAT minimum in the datasheet is 3.5 V

Choice: ER-OLED0.96-1.3W

Rationale: The hub UI only has to show temperature and audio status. A 128 x 64 SSD1306 module does that, costs $2.49, and does not have the 12- and 16-week lead times of the larger panels. Option 2 also needs 12.5 V, which this board does not have. The FPC module is the intentional exception to the through-hole preference. It mates with an EastRising ER-CON30HT-1, a 30-pin, 0.5 mm, top-contact ZIF.

docs.title: 9 V to 5 V Regulator
docs.text:
Requirements: Make a regulated 5 V rail from the 9 V barrel jack for the Curiosity Nano, the debug LED, and the current that the 3.3 V regulator draws. The package should be through-hole. The part must stay in regulation at 9 V and at the budgeted load, and the heat has to be acceptable without treating the regulator as an efficient converter.

The generic name "7805" is the 5 V family. The part selected for U4 is the Fairchild LM7805CT, a through-hole TO-220 regulator at $1.74.

docs.title: Option 1: L7805CV (STMicroelectronics)
docs.text:
• ~$1.08 each
  • Link to product
  • ST L78 datasheet
Pros Cons Fixed 5 V, TO-220, through-hole Linear regulator: the drop from 9 V to 5 V becomes heat Output current up to 1.5 A Quiescent current up to 8 mA at 25 °C 9 V is inside the 7 V to 18 V test range used for the 5 V specification up to 1 A Minimum load for regulation is 5 mA Datasheet test circuit uses 0.33 µF in and 0.1 µF out, which is what the schematic already has (C9, C10) Dropout is typically 2 V at 1 A and 25 °C, so it is not a low-dropout part

docs.title: Option 2: MCP1702T-5002E/CB (Microchip)
docs.text:
• ~$0.65 each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons Very low quiescent current 250 mA maximum output Good for battery operation SOT-23, not through-hole Accepts up to 13.2 V input Less common than the 7805 family High DigiKey stock

This option is a 5.0 V LDO. It is not the 3.3 V regulator selected later.

docs.title: Option 3: MC7805CDTRKG (onsemi)
docs.text:
• ~$0.49 each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons Same 7805 family, 5 V output Linear, so it also dissipates (9 V − 5 V) × Iout Low cost DPAK, not through-hole Up to 1 A output Harder to hand solder than TO-220

Choice: LM7805CT

  • $1.74 each
  • Link to product

Rationale: The hub needs a through-hole 5 V regulator from the 9 V jack. The LM7805CT is available in TO-220 and is the part on the bill of materials. The L7805CV is ST's TO-220 part in the same family and was kept as the closest compared alternative. The MCP1702 was set aside because it is SOT-23 and its maximum output is 250 mA. The MC7805CDTRKG was set aside because it is DPAK. The budgeted 5 V current, after the 25% margin, is 71.625 mA. A 7805 is linear, so the drop from 9 V to 5 V becomes heat. That heat is small at this load, which is why a linear regulator is acceptable here.

docs.title: I2C Level-Shift MOSFET
docs.text:
Requirements: SDA and SCL have to cross between the 5 V PIC pins and the 3.3 V OLED pins. Two N-channel, through-hole MOSFETs are used, one for each line.

Choice: two onsemi 2N7000, Q1 and Q2

  • $0.65 each
  • 2N7000 on DigiKey
  • onsemi 2N7000 datasheet

Rationale: The 2N7000 is inexpensive, widely stocked, and commonly used for this kind of I2C level shift. One device is used on SDA and one on SCL.

docs.title: 5 V to 3.3 V Regulator
docs.text:
Requirements: A second regulator has to make 3.3 V from the 5 V rail for the OLED. It needs a fixed 3.3 V output and a through-hole package. The display load used in the power budget is 32.3 mA.

Choice: MCP1700-3302E/TO

  • $0.50 each
  • Fixed 3.3 V, TO-92, 250 mA
  • MCP1700-3302E/TO on DigiKey
  • Microchip MCP1700 datasheet

Rationale: The MCP1700-3302E/TO is inexpensive, widely stocked, and a common through-hole 3.3 V regulator. It supplies the OLED from the 5 V rail.

docs.title: MCC Configuration
docs.text:
The hub uses the PIC18F57Q43 on the Curiosity Nano. The clock is the internal HFINTOSC. There is no external crystal on the schematic. Peripheral pin select maps the digital pins below.

Function Peripheral Pins System clock HFINTOSC Internal OLED I2C, after the 2N7000 shifters I2C SDA on RB2, SCL on RB1 Debug LED PWM RA2 UART connector 1 UART TX on RC2, RX on RC3 UART connector 2 UART TX on RF0, RX on RF1 UART connector 3 UART TX on RA3, RX on RA4 Debug button GPIO input SW1

The three UART ports link this hub to the microphone board, the button and temperature board, and the speaker board. I2C is shifted from 5 V at the microcontroller to 3.3 V at the OLED by Q1 and Q2. SW1 is the debug button on this board. The user buttons are on board 2.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic is the RadioLink hub for Team 105. The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano reads the microphone board and the button and temperature board over UART, shows the interface on the ER-OLED0.96-1.3W, and sends the microphone signal to the speaker board.

Power comes from a 9 V barrel jack, through a 1 A fuse, into an LM7805CT that makes the 5 V rail. An MCP1700-3302E/TO makes 3.3 V from that rail for the display. Two 2N7000 MOSFETs level-shift I2C between the 5 V microcontroller and the 3.3 V display. A debug LED and a debug button sit on this board. The user controls stay on board 2.

Figure 1: Hub subsystem schematic.

docs.title: Function
docs.text:
RadioLink needs one board that can collect the microphone and the button and temperature data, show it, and pass the microphone audio to the speaker. This schematic is that board.

Three UART connectors are the links to the other boards. One brings in the microphone, one brings in the pushbuttons and the temperature reading, and one carries the microphone signal out to the speaker. Those links are logic-level RX and TX. They do not power the other boards.

The ER-OLED0.96-1.3W is the interface the user sees. It plugs into an ER-CON30HT-1 top-contact ZIF. Board 2's buttons move through that screen. Q1 and Q2 level-shift SDA and SCL so the 5 V microcontroller can talk to the 3.3 V display. JP1 can open the display supply without shutting off the rest of the hub.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This budget is for the RadioLink hub only. It covers the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, the EastRising ER-OLED0.96-1.3W, the debug LED, the LM7805CT, and the MCP1700-3302E/TO. The microphone, button, and speaker boards are not included. Their UART links are logic-level signals, and those boards carry their own supplies.

The 9 V barrel jack feeds the LM7805CT. The 5 V rail feeds the PIC, the debug LED, and the MCP1700. The 3.3 V rail feeds the display. A linear regulator does not remove the load current. The MCP1700 input current is still a load on the 5 V rail, and that 5 V current is still a load on the 9 V input.

Currents below are datasheet limits or the allowances already used on this page. They are not lab measurements. The 25% margin is kept on each regulated rail. Quiescent current is included where the datasheet maximum is large enough to matter.

docs.title: Display current
docs.text:
The orderable display is the ER-OLED0.96-1.3W. SSD1306 is the controller on that module. EastRising Note 8 lists a maximum IBAT of 32.0 mA with the internal charge pump, VDD = 2.8 V, generated VCC = 7.25 V, and 100% of the pixels on. IDD maximum is 300 µA. Those two maxima add to:

32.0 mA + 0.3 mA = 32.3 mA

32.3 mA is the sum of those published maxima.

docs.title: Rails
docs.text:
Figure 1: Loads on the 5 V rail and the 3.3 V rail, including the 25% margin.

Figure 2: Current drawn from the 9 V barrel jack, including the 8 mA quiescent allowance.

docs.title: 3.3 V rail
docs.text:
The only 3.3 V load in this budget is the display, at 32.3 mA.

Margined current = 32.3 mA × 1.25 = 40.375 mA

The MCP1700-3302E/TO is rated for 250 mA when the output is 2.5 V or higher. Remaining capacity is 250 mA − 40.375 mA = 209.625 mA.

Load power and regulator loss at the 32.3 mA datasheet sum, not at the margin, are:

P_load = 3.3 V × 0.0323 A = 0.1066 W

P_MCP1700 = (5.0 V − 3.3 V) × 0.0323 A = 0.0549 W

P_input ≈ 5.0 V × 0.0323 A + 5.0 V × 4 µA = 0.1615 W

The 4 µA term is the MCP1700 maximum quiescent current. It does not change the milliamp total. TO-92 thermal resistance in the MCP1700 datasheet is 92 °C/W, so 0.0549 W is about a 5 °C rise.

docs.title: 5 V rail
docs.text:
Load Current PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano allowance 15 mA Debug LED allowance, D4 with R7 = 330 Ω 10 mA MCP1700 input, equal to the 32.3 mA display current 32.3 mA Subtotal 57.3 mA After 25% margin 71.625 mA

The 15 mA PIC number is the operating allowance used for 5 V operation with UART, I2C, and PWM. The 10 mA LED allowance is for the Lite-On LTL-4293, whose typical forward voltage is 2.0 V at 10 mA, with R7 = 330 Ω.

The 5 V regulator is the LM7805CT. This budget uses a 7805-family estimate: 1.5 A output capability, 8 mA quiescent current, and 50 °C/W for the TO-220 package.

That 1.5 A rating leaves 1.5 A − 71.625 mA = 1.428 A. The 1 A fuse is on the 9 V input, not on the 5 V output.

At the margined 71.625 mA output current, using that 8 mA quiescent maximum:

P_LM7805 = (9 V − 5 V) × 0.071625 A + 9 V × 0.008 A = 0.359 W

At 50 °C/W the rise is about 18 °C. Output power is 5 V × 0.071625 A = 0.358 W. Input power is 9 V × (0.071625 A + 0.008 A) = 0.717 W. Efficiency is 0.358 / 0.717 = 50%. The LM7805 is appropriate in this estimate because the heat is small, not because a linear drop from 9 V to 5 V is efficient.

docs.title: 9 V input
docs.text:
Current from the barrel jack is the margined 5 V output current plus the 8 mA quiescent maximum:

71.625 mA + 8 mA = 79.625 mA

The fuse is 1 A, so the unused current is 1000 mA − 79.625 mA = 920.375 mA. The speaker amplifier stays on board 3. USB on the Curiosity Nano can power the microcontroller during programming, and that path is separate from this 9 V budget.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: The margined hub load is 71.625 mA on the 5 V rail and 40.375 mA on the 3.3 V rail. Against the 1.5 A 7805-family figure used above, and the MCP1700 250 mA rating, both loads are small. LM7805CT dissipation at the margined load is 0.359 W. MCP1700 dissipation at the 32.3 mA display sum is 0.0549 W. The 9 V input, limited by the 1 A fuse, still has 920 mA of spare current. The speaker amplifier stays on board 3.
